speechtext:
I should like to ask
one or two questions at this point. Last Friday, referring to the milling industry, the minister told the committee that if sixty per cent of that industry in the province of Ontario desired to come under this proposed legislation the remaining forty per cent could be compelled to come under it as well. I should like to ask the minister as to the basis upon which the percentage will be decided. I assume the capacity of the mills will have to be considered. Then when you take the big milling companies such as the Lake of the Woods, the Ogilvie company and others, they have a still larger capacity. On what basis will that percentage be decided? Will it be on the basis of capacity?
While I am on my feet I should like to ask another question, this time in regard to the produce sold on the markets of the larger towns and cities in the province of Ontario. Will the local board have the right to say whether the farmers can bring to the markets certain products such as chickens, eggs, butter and so on, and will the board have power to say that a farmer may come in to-day but that he may not come in next week, just because they say he cannot? I should like some information from the minister in that regard.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING N ATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
My hon. friend's
questions are alike in this respect, that each matter will have to be dealt with on its own merits on the basis of the scheme submitted by the producers themselves. If they submit a certain scheme which is approved
by the provincial government then it will be a matter for the jurisdiction of that government.

speechtext:
I should like to ask
the minister if the local board will have full jurisdiction in regard to the marketing of produce on the local markets. Will the local board have the right to say whether certain products should be marketed on a certain day?

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING N ATURAL PRODUCTS

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING N ATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Then going back to
the milling industry, from the answers given by the minister on Friday last I take it that the milling industry would be under the jurisdiction of three boards, the dominion board, the provincial board and the local board.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING N ATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: I did not intend to leave the impression that such an industry would be under three boards. It depends entirely on the plan or policy they suggest. It might be provincial or interprovincial, or it might deal only with exports.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING N ATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
That answer is all
right as far as it goes, but it is still vague to me. I should like to know how these boards are to be appointed. Coming first to the local board, who appoints that board?

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING N ATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: That is provided for in one of the clauses of the act. It depends upon the way in which the scheme is submitted. The business of the appointment of the board is so closely related to the scheme submitted by the producers that one could not state definitely in each case how a board would be appointed. In a general way I would say the answer would be this, that when the producers submit their scheme they have to state in that scheme how they wish the board to be appointed. It might be an election by the producers themselves. It might be that the board they would like to have set up would consist of a majority of producers, but also a certain number of people in the trade and, in connection with apples, shippers. Also they may ask for representation from a consumer body, or by one member of the government. But it depends entirely upon the plan they have evolved and wish to put into effect.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING N ATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
I am not very much enlightened. Perhaps I did not put my
Marketing Act

question in a way capable of being understood by the minister. In order to make myself as clear as possible may I ask this question: Will the dominion board have control over the provincial board and the local board, or will the dominion board have control of the provincial board and the provincial board have control of the local board?

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING N ATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: It depends entirely on what scheme is suggested. A local board may be set up to deal purely with the matter of marketing, or the regulation of marketing within the province. That might be under the provincial government. The dominion board may, under certain conditions, use and name a provincial board to carry out the plan submitted for interprovincial and export trade, while for trade within the province the regulation might be under the jurisdiction of the province. My answer may not be as definite as the hon. member would wish-

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING N ATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: I am sorry to say it is not very definite.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING N ATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: What I am trying to explain to the hon. member is that no person can decide until the case is placed before him. Each case will have to be decided on its own merits.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING N ATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: I am sorry to say the minister's explanation is not very clear to me, although it may be clear to some other hon. members in the committee. Let me take the milling industry as an example. In connection with that industry there are three classes of customers, if I may so describe them. The industry has its local trade dealing in flour, it has customers in other provinces and it has a large export trade. Will the milling industry be under the control of three boards, namely, the local board, the provincial board and the dominion board? May I point out that in the flour industry orders are usually received by cable. The dealers cable price quotations, acceptances or non-acceptances. In the event of an acceptance of a shipment of flour to be sent to Great Britain, or to any other point outside of Canada, will the millers first have to consult the local board, the provincial board or the dominion board before they may close the order?

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING N ATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: Or the celestial board?

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING N ATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
It depends on what plan they submit. They may submit a plan to regulate milling in connection with export trade, only. That would be under a local

board, set up with the approval of the dominion board by the milling industry itself. If the proposition were one affecting only marketing within the province it could be under provincial jurisdiction.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING N ATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: Well then, will the provincial governments appoint the local boards?

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING N ATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
It depends on the
scheme submitted. In submitting the scheme they have to state how they wish the board selected, whether by election from their own people, the people submitting the proposition, or anly partially from those people to act along with other representatives to be selected by the province-if it is purely a provincial matter-or by the dominion if it is a matter of export.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING N ATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
I shall put another
question to the minister concerning the jurisdiction of local boards. Let us consider the local butchers who buy their supply from nearby farmers. Will they have to obtain permission from a local board before they may buy beef on the hoof for killing purposes, and to offer for sale in a local butcher shop?

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING N ATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: That depends entirely under what scheme they may be working, and the scheme submitted.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING N ATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: Well then, would the minister go just a little farther. Surely he can tell the committee a little more about the scheme, and the whole process. So far as I am concerned-and it may be my own fault-for the life of me I cannot obtain enlightenment in this matter.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING N ATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: I am afraid the hon. member has not yet grasped what the bill in this particular, means.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING N ATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: Nobody else has.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING N ATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: The bill sets out that the producers or the people interested in the formation of a local board to regulate the marketing of their products will submit a scheme which they think will work out in their own best interests, and towards the better regulation of that product. They submit a scheme, but no person now knows what the scheme may be.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING N ATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: Not even the minister.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING N ATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: No, not even the minister.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING N ATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
So we are voting on something we do not know anything about-

Marketing Act

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING N ATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: No, we are not voting on something we do not know about. We are voting on something that I have endeavoured to make clear over and over again, namely that the producers themselves, by organization in so far as they may indicate should be given authority over the control and regulation of their own products. Under different circumstances different producers will submit different schemes. Those schemes will be laid before the dominion board, investigated and then laid before the governor in council or the lieutenant governor in council. But such scheme can operate only in so far as authority is given by this legislation.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING N ATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: From the last answer the minister has given I take it that the dominion board will have jurisdiction and control over the provincial and local boards.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING N ATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: No, not necessarily. For instance, the Fraser river valley milk producers may want to submit a scheme for the marketing of their products within the province of British Columbia. That need not necessarily be referred to the dominion board or the dominion government.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING N ATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: One more question in regard to local creameries. Before a local creamery may make a sale of butter or cheese will it have to obtain the consent of the local and provincial boards?

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING N ATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: It depends entirely on what system they may want to follow.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING N ATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: How many systems will there be?

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING N ATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: It depends on the producers themselves. The producers in each locality, each province or, as in the case of live stock, in the dominion, would submit what they think would be the best way to regulate the marketing of their own products.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING N ATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: Well then someone has to work out those schemes.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING N ATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: Yes, certainly; the producers submit their own schemes.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING N ATURAL PRODUCTS

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING N ATURAL PRODUCTS

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING N ATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: I should like to ask a question pertaining to the appointments of these boards. Must the boards, either local or provincial, appointed to any scheme meet the point of view of the minister? I know the dominion board would.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING N ATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: Not necessarily, so far as personnel is concerned. For instance, a body of producers would ask that a local board be elected to consist entirely of the producers, themselves. They elect their own board, and are responsible for the personnel of it. But the scheme must be approved by the minister, either provincial or federal, before the local board can be appointed and the scheme go into effect.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING N ATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: Suppose the producers submitting a scheme decide that they are going to have only producers on the board and that the minister disagrees. Has he the right to set aside such a decision and say that so far as the marketing of grain, for instance, is concerned, the trade must be represented? Suppose the producers do not want the trade represented on the board; has the minister then power to say to the producers that that is not right or fair, or to give them some reason why some other representative should sit on the board?

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING N ATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: That is all part of the scheme which has to be approved by the minister, but the hon. member I think will agree that if a body sufficiently representative of the producers and sufficiently representative also of the production submit a scheme that is approved, the personnel of the board would not be a major point of issue.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING N ATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: Is there any safeguard there for the consumers?

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING N ATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: I would say that there are three safeguards: first, that the scheme has to be approved by the minister and by the governor in council; second, that there is no price fixing but a regulating of the rate at which the stuff goes on to the market; third, there is part II of the act which gives power to control undue charges.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING N ATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
The consumer
would not be represented on any of the boards contemplated?

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING N ATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
That depends entirely on the scheme submitted by the producers. In the first draft of the bill we had a provision for representation of producers, the trade, and consumers on the local board. It is a matter for the producers submitting the scheme to designate whether or not they wish consumers represented on the board, but I think producers have reached the stage where they fully realize that the good will of the public is essential in the marketing and regulating of their products. Personally I would say that the consumers would be more protected under this act than they are at present.

speechtext:
(Ontario): Speaking on May 8, the minister stated:
I am answering the statement which the hon. member for Ontario made decrying very strenuously the principle of compulsory cooperation. I could give numerous similar examples throughout the dominion where members of a community bind themselves together because the majority feel that it would be of advantage to have compulsory cooperation. For instance, I might cite the building of roads.
Then later on the minister, referring to the member for Ontario, says:
If we follow the argument advanced by the hon. member for Ontario, I suppose he would advocate that each farmer in a community should make his own trail and build his own road to town so that he might thereby retain his own individuality and initiative.
Now, Mr. Chairman, so far as the farmers of my county are concerned, the county which I represent with an honoured colleague on the other side of the house, that is precisely what many of the producers of my county do. They and their fathers have built trails, out of many years of hard work and honest service-trails to their own markets. I want to know from the minister if the vote of any group of men is to destroy what they have done. They have sold, and still sell direct to the consumers. Many of them sell to the merchants. Is it possible that we are passing legislation to enable any body of producers to wipe out what they have built? May I go a little bit further?
The producers of my county are business men. I think my colleague who sits on the other side of the house will say that some of them are very able business men. Are they to be deprived of the privilege of conducting their own business? Many of them have sold their products under farm names, and those farm names stand for quality of goods, for integrity of service. Many of them have registered brand names. Are those brands to be wiped out by the vote of other producers? To me the matter seems almost incomprehensible.
The minister has taken the parallel of the road. Are these producers to be forced, blindfolded, down the common road? The other day in this house the Minister of Trade and Commerce referred to the wiping out of the services rendered by the captains of industry through the operation of finance, through the working of mergers. He said that we had lost the direction of five hundred men who knew industry and had been accustomed to direct it. I agree with the minister that was a very serious loss. But under this bill are we to wipe out the initiative of hundreds of thousands of farmers and central-

ize it in the hands and under the direction of any group of marketing boards?

I doubt whether there is any need for panic. I am either right or wrong in thinking this bill, if made law, will bring about an economic revolution. It is very easy to shout "red;" it is very easy to make such statements as I have made, but will the minister tell me: What is the history of the bill? What is the history of legislation of this kind? He has made that very plain; he says:
Queensland was perhaps the pioneer state in this system of cooperative marketing.
What was the background in Queensland? The minister, who is a graduate of the university from which I graduated, is familiar with social questions. He will remember the name of William Lane, a man who conducted in Queensland an agitation and almost brought about a revolution for communism in the latter part of the last century, an eloquent, honest, misguided man. The minister will remember the uprising that followed in Queensland and the horrors which were perpetrated. He will remember that Lane carried a group of his followers to Paraguay and there founded a new Australia, and when the tide in Queensland subsided, it left this form of legislation. Founded on communism, Queensland was the pioneer state of socialism. Mr. A. St. Ledger, a senator in Queensland, writing on the subject of Australian Socialism, pointed that out very clearly. He said:
Socialism had its origin in Queensland. From Queensland it took its inspiration. The Worker was the press exponent of the spirit of that socialism.

Marketing Act-Mr. Moore (Ontario)
The Worker, by the way was the organ of Mr. Lane.
It undertook to explain to Australia what socialism meant, and what was its spirit.
That was the background of this legislation. How did it come about? It came about for this reason: the people decided that it was a government function to fix wages. Not marketing, mind you, not first. It was a government function to fix wages. The farmers in Australia had many employees. Having passed that legislation then the government was obliged to pass legislation fixing a wage fund. This government has the cart before the horse.
Now for the benefit of myhon. friends to my left and for the information of the minister may I say that Queensland was the pioneer cooperative commonwealth. I am not an authority; it may have had its genesis before this time, but in 1905 a labour convention met at Brisbane in Queensland. Mr. Reinhold, who was a member of the legislature, moved the following resolution:
That the objective of the labour movement is the establishment of a cooperative commonwealth by the furtherance in national, state, and municipal legislation of the following principles:-
(a)	In "politics," the principles of democracy. Complete self-government vested in the people, every adult standing on equality at the ballot box.
(b)	In economics, the principles of collectivism. The scientific organization of labour; the equitable distribution of the product of labour by the nation, state, and municipality owning and cooperating, in .the interests of all its citizens, the monopolies and large industries of the community.
That is the background of this sort of legislation. That is the birthplace. Well, there is another remarkable parallel. We have here a union of forces back of this bill. Surely there is a difference in the object of coercion. I can see where a man should be coerced to the extent of being prevented from selling bad eggs, but it is a different thing from coercing him from selling eggs at all. I can see where I should be coerced not to take another man's property, but it is a different thing when I am coerced in the use of my own property. They have realized how difficult- impossible, in fact-it was for them to act as individuals, and to get what was coming to them: hence the formation of cooperatives. My hon. friend knows perfectly well that years ago a very large number of farmers in the prairie provinces realized it was impossible to carry out a purely voluntary scheme, and advocated a hundred per cent wheat pool. For the moment I am not discussing whether or not this bill is all that it should be, but I do say that the principle of coercion is one to which we are accustomed in other spheres.
Let me take, for example, the cattle business. I live in the city of Winnipeg and

Marketing Act-Mr. Woodsworth
know some of the farmers in that district. They have told me about driving cattle to Winnipeg, or shipping them by truck or railway, and receiving only $5 or $10 for an animal which had cost $15 or $20 to raise. Under the circumstances what could they do other than accept the price offered by the cattle buyers? It is quite true that if they had driven the beast in they could have driven it home again, but their expenses would have been too high. Under present conditions the producer is almost helpless. A buyer came to see me last year and told me that he had attempted to secure poultry to ship to the British market. After receiving an order he made an effort to obtain a carload of poultry. He travelled from place to place, from farm to farm, finally from Winnipeg to Saskatoon, and after going through some rather shady transactions and splitting his order into three or four parts he managed to obtain a carload of poultry to send to the British market. Those were his difficulties, so strong was the monopoly, and so impossible was it for him to break the monopoly which existed at that time.
I do not think we need discuss the question of tobacco, which has been reviewed before the price spreads committee. I should like to know in view of the situation which has been found to exist in Ontario what possible freedom of action is possessed by the individual grower. The fact is that we are living under a set of conditions that make remarks such as those made by the hon. member for Ontario absolutely ridiculous, more than ridiculous, because he is talking of conditions that existed fifty years ago. His remarks do not apply to conditions as they exist to-day.
The same is true with regard to his suggestion about a man having a right to his own private property. I have said in this house before, and I should like to repeat, that it seems to me the time has come when we shall have to redefine what private property is. I take it from its derivation that private property should mean those things which I can use and enjoy for myself. It has to do essentially with personal matters. But the lawyers have stretched its meaning. They have created an artificial body which they have called a corporation, and they have endowed that corporation with nearly all the attributes of an individual. They have said that the corporation can hold private property. It is an altogether unwarrantable extension of the term, and so we have these great corporations and trusts to-day holding what they call "private property." The result is that it is an absolute impossibility for me to have any effective control over my
private property in the face of the strength which these big corporations exercise in the economic sphere.
We who have been accustomed to the straits in which the labour people find themselves have had this borne in upon us over and over again. In the old days a man had the opportunity to work with his own hands and sell the product of his labour, but unfortunately very few people have that opportunity to-day, for the vast number of people are working under the wages system. They are employees of someone else. They have not the right to sell the product of their own hands. The best they can do is to receive a wage, and somebody else takes the product off their hands and sells it for them, but actual producers having no voice in its sale and really having no right to say how much of what has been produced shall be kept by themselves. That is the situation that exists, and under these circumstances this idea that we axe losing something of our private initiative and sacrificing our private property is all nonsense.
The same is true of free trade. It was all very well a hundred years ago to have free trade when the indivdual was producing with his own equipment and in free competition with other individuals, but we know perfectly well to-day that we no longer produce as individuals. We produce in what is essentially forced cooperation in a great factory. I say forced cooperation because in order to earn a living a man must go into the factory where there may be one thousand or ten thousand employees all working together, cooperating if you like, but it is forced cooperation under the lash of economic necessity. Well, under those circumstances it is futile to talk about competition in the old sense or about free trade in the old sense. At best it is free competition only between big industries and free trade only between huge corporations. Superimposed upon that we must remember that we have arrangements existing with regard to prices, tariffs, gentlemen's agreements, and what not. Free trade under those circumstances becomes an almost meaningless term.
Competition is the life of trade-that is what we used to be taught and we wrote it in our copy books, if I remember right, but today Mr. Beatty of the Canadian Pacific Railway comes along and tells us that there must be some sort of unification of administration of our railroads, that competition means waste, and I think Mr. Beatty is right, that ultimately competition does mean waste. It is a question in each particular case to decide if

Marketing Act-Mr. Woodsworth
it is worth while to adopt a system that does mean waste. But when we have reduced our competition between the railways to competition between two systems only, the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National, and Mr. Beatty, a recognized authority, comes along and tells us that even that measure of competition is wrong and that we should have unification in order to eliminate waste and promote efficiency, then I say we may well ask whether we shall not have to reconstruct our ideas and bring our policies up to modern ways of conducting business.
The member for Ontario, as I said earlier, is essentially an anarchist in his thinking. He does not believe in the reign of law. He holds up the horrors of socialism. But what is socialism after all? It is simply the doctrine that the interests of society should be given precedence over the interests of predatory individuals. That is all. Surely we have reached that stage when the interests of the community at large or the interests of very large sections of the community ought to have the right of way over the selfish interests of comparatively small groups.

speechtext: I said that it is another camouflage for democracy.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING N ATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
I take it that
democracy, according to its root meaning, means the rule of the people. We have had a certain amount, of the rule of the people when it comes to what we have termed purely political matters, freedom of speech, the right to vote, and so on, and I give all credit to the historic Liberal party for having won us a certain amount of constitutional freedom along that line. But there are other lines along which we have not yet attained democracy, the rule of the people. You go into any industry to-day, and industry managed by a great corporation, under a manager who is all-powerful, and will you tell me that there is any rule of the people in that industry? The rule of the people would mean that the employees are given some rights in that industry, that they have something to say about hours of labour, the wages they are paid, the profits gained, and have some share in the division of profits. That would be the rule of the people within that industry. But industry has remained outside of democracy. Industry to-day is an autocracy, and industry is suffering to-day because it is an autocracy.

It seems to me that in some way we shall have to introduce principles of democracy into industry.
The same thing is true of our commerce. This committee on price spreads is simply revealing in a public way what a good many of us knew before existed, that we had autocracy in our commerce, and that under the present conditions people were suffering. I do not think we can go back to the old idea that each tobacco producer, we will say, can himself see that his goods reach the final consumer. I think that is an impossibility. Under these circumstances we have to arrange *that the producers 'have some sort of protection, some sort of help in arranging their cooperative enterprises so as to gain the full results of their production and through the cutting out of the middle man be enabled to participate in the marketing of their products.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING N ATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: What are you going to do with the middle men?

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING N ATURAL PRODUCTS

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING N ATURAL PRODUCTS

No. I would say that undoubtedly there is a function to be performed by the man who stands between the producer and the consumer. I would refer hon. gentlemen to the splendid work that has been done by the cooperative societies in Great Britain. They have recognized the necessity of cooperation over there, and they have employed managers to carry on their business in an efficient way. They have themselves engaged in production, setting decent minimum standards of living for those engaged in production. It is quite possible that they may show us the way to carry this out.
I am criticizing this bill because it does not safeguard the interests of the consumers. Theoretically I might approach this whole problem from the standpoint of the consumer rather than of the producer but I must deal with matters as they now stand. The producers axe in a very bad way and I think we are doing the logical thing by safeguarding their interests. It may be that ultimately we will have to approach this problem from the standpoint of the consumer rather than of the producer but in the meanwhile we axe providing for certain minimum standards which

Marketing Act-Mr. Mullins
the producer cannot obtain without some help from the state.
When I was interrupted a few minutes ago I was about to say that it seems to me that in the realm of finance we are still under an autocracy. I do not know of any better confirmation of this fact than the statement made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) a few weeks ago when the central bank bill was under discussion. He said that if there was a difference of opinion or of policy between the government and the new central bank, the opinion and policy of the central bank would prevail over that of the Minister of Finance and the govenment. As I tried to point out at the time, that simply means that we are legalizing the autocracy which exists in the financial world. I take it that in the financial as well as the commercial 'world we shall have to introduce principles of real democracy. I think some of the principles which I have been trying to advocate show that I believe in democracy far more than the Liberals; that I believe in freedom far more than the Liberals, and I would urge upon them that the principles of Liberalism, the principles of freedom and the principles of democracy have to be worked out under twentieth century conditions and not under nineteenth century conditions. I give credit to the Conservatives that in this bill they are attempting to do more than the Liberals have done.

Mr. Chairman, I have not taken up much of the time of the committee as I realize it costs $41 per minute to conduct the business of parliament, it is not my intention to take up very much time now. I have listened to the pros and cons of this discussion; I have listened to the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Moore), but much as I would like to agree with him, I cannot. I realize the appalling situation facing agriculture in western Canada and I am prepared to support this bill if it will assist agriculture out of the morass and mess in which it is at the present time.
A lot has been said about cooperation. At one time I opposed cooperation more than any other hon. member, but later on I became converted. I mean cooperation without exploitation. It is not cooperation when a man exploits the public by getting a good position and obtaining his pound of flesh. I want the same kind of cooperation that we had in Glasgow. When the cooperative system was first proposed there, I opposed it most strongly. I refused to sell my cattle to the cooperative
but finally I found myself trading with them and I discovered it to be a really good system. The hon. member for South Battleford (Mr. Vallance) knows the success which has been made with that system in Glasgow and I am sure he is familiar with the stores scattered all over the city.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING N ATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: But it is a voluntary system.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING N ATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
It is true cooperation. After I was defeated in 1926 I went to California. At that time I heard a great evangelist over the radio and this is what he said: Labour, you have a perfect right to be organized as long as the men at the head of your organization are not leading you to some place politically in order that they may obtain fat positions. Farmers, you have a perfect right to be organized, he said: I am one of you, but I think we are the biggest fools that ever went into organization. I had ten acres of walnuts near Los Angeles and every year my wife and I shook hands when we received $1,600 yearly for our walnuts. But a young man came around one day and wanted me to join a cooperative organization and since that time my wife and I have not shaken hands. I am now getting $400 per year for my walnuts while this young man draws $30,000 per year and he does not know walnuts from hickory nuts.
The same thing is what was wrong with western Canada. You had your Mr. Crerar, a gentleman who occupied a seat in this house. His company organized the farmers in the cattle business, but what was the result? The hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown) can tell the committee.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING N ATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: Yes, I can.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING N ATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
You can tell the results when you get up to speak. What was the result of organizing the farmers in the cattle business? They engaged incompetent men and could not carry on the marketing of their products. I am going to support the minister although I will admit that at first I was afraid of this bill. I did not like cooperation in Scotland when they brought it out, but I was converted. We are living in changed times. Last Sunday morning I listened to the minister of Yorkminster church in the city of Toronto. He said that in his time there would be no poverty, the change would come about by evolution and revolution. I spoke to him about using the word "revolution" but he said: I did not mean brickbats and rifles, I meant a revolution of the
Marketing Act-Mr. Mullins

heart. Things to-day are not the same as they were in the old days of fifty years ago, conditions have changed.
I can remember when I used to go into the field and ask a farmer what he wanted for his cattle. He wanted so much, I would make a bid and we arrived at a bargain. But some men have gone through the country to get the farmers to ship their products to the packer and let the packer set the price. The initiative has been taken away from the farmer. He now loads his cattle into a truck and they go to the packer's yard and the packer does the weighing, the grading and sets the price. All hon. members need to do is read the evidence given in the Stevens committee. I think the old system was the best. I admit that I liked it but I realize also that times have changed. While I am getting grey I think I have the right to measure up the situation as it is facing us to-day.
They say this is the young man's age, but I think the old days were the best. In the old days we had our pipes and were not spending $50,000,000 every year on cigarettes. We were not blowing up $50,000,000 a year in smoke. I think of the old family doctor and then I think of the specialist we have to-day who reaches into your pocket book and takes your last dollar before he operates on you. I think of the old storekeeper in my constituency of Marquette, which I am proud to represent, a purely agricultural constituency, not a single manufacture in it. I think of the little towns, smaller to-day than they were forty years ago, withering up through the new systems of buying and marketing. Those systems were wrong but I believe the system proposed will help the farmer particularly along two lines, and I want to mention them. Does the committee realize what is meant by the provision in the bill for the regulation of importation of products? I have not heard a word about this from the other side of the house. Why do hon. members opposite not speak of the way in which this measure will regulate the importation of products?
Do hon. members know that Canada is importing equal to 17,000 head of cattle from the Argentine? Do they know that there are being brought in all the old, decrepit cattle, all the rubbish of the Argentine ranges, in the way of canned meats that can be found on the shelves in our retail stores? I say: Heaven help the mothers of to-day who become can openers. I wonder whether in the ladies' college, when they were giving them their degree in domestic science, they presented them with gold-headed can openers. I think

of the old times when our mothers knew how to cook a roast of beef. I have in my hand a can of meat; I took the label off it; I did not intend to bring it into the house but I may say that I bought it in Ottawa. It represents part of the product of many thousands of cattle in the Argentine. I ask those who have used this canned meat: Do you know what it is composed of? It is made of the worst class of animals on the range. I dare not mention on the floor of the house some of the animals that are inside these cans of meat, yet some mothers will open them and use the contents. I would like to go further along this line but I say to the minister that if he will put into effect that part of the bill providing for the regulation of the importation of those meats and also vegetable oils that are coming into Canada millions will be saved to the farmers of the dominion as a result.
We are bringing in cottonseed oil, with the odour taken out of it by the Wesson process, letting it go into our packing plants and be sold to the people to replace lard. Every time you eat fried potatoes, just think you are eating cottonseed oil, the product of the southern states, deodorized by a system called the Wesson system. I have before me a list of the other products that are being imported and it is appalling.
I am in favour of real cooperation and I wonder why my hon. friends opposite are opposing it. They are trying to get political cooperation in the constituency of Marquette; they want the Liberals and Progressives to cooperate. Then why are they opposing this bill? I have before me the report of a meeting in my principal town, Minnedosa, and it says "Cooperation between the Progressives and the Liberals." I would say to my hon. friends opposite in an advisory way: Go out as good, honest Liberals and contest the seat. If my right hon. friend gets those Progressive Liberals tacked on to him and he comes into power at the next election, he has my sympathy; I will come here and sympathize with him because when he spoke at Kentville, Nova Scotia, at Moose Jaw, Calgary and all over western Canada, he did not want those people tacked on to him and yet in Minnedosa my hon. friends opposite want cooperation. I may say that I cut this clipping out of the Free Press yesterday. A gentleman by the name of Linden outlines the Liberal policy at Minnedosa, but I find my friend Mr. J. Allison Glenn, who used to occupy the seat before me, he is with him and says that there should be cooperation as Liberal Progressives. That is the cooperation

Marketing Act-Mr. Mackenzie King
they are trying to put into effect in Marquette.
If this bill will go toward aiding agriculture I am willing to give it a trial. Why do my hon. friends opposite not do the same thing? If they knew the true situation on the prairies, of the struggling masses engaged in agriculture in the west, as I do, I am sure they would support legislation which is intended to help to bring back normal conditions in the west.
There are many evils we can remedy. I am opposed to the excessively high rates of interest that are being charged by the various corporations in the big cities who have exploited the poor farmer and kept him down. They have had their pound of flesh but today there is danger in sight for them. They are not going to get the same rates of interest as they charged before. Having said that much, I am not going to take up any more of the time of the committee as I do realize the amount of money that it costs to keep this house in session. I appeal to my Liberal friends-and I have many of them on the other side whom I respect very much-that they give some opportunity to the struggling masses. Never mind whether it comes from the far southeast corner of the house or not; it does not make any difference who is supporting it. At first, when I found that the hon. member for Melville (Mr. Motherwell) was supporting this legislation, I was afraid there was something wrong with it, because he and I have been fighting political battles for the last forty years. I would like to take his hand and let us walk in together and say that we meet on common ground. I ask my hon. friends to give this bill a trial in the interests of the struggling masses of the west as stated.

The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woods-worth) spoke at some length of the necessity of compulsion and coercion in all matters of government. May I say that I agree with him that where you have government intervention you must have behind it the power to compel obedience, but in justifying intervention, and the compulsion by which it is enforced, everything depends upon the purpose to be served by compulsion, in other words the purpose of the intervention. The hon. member has cited a number of instances which, he says, illustrate what he has in mind. He has spoken of the community in which he lives, in which a waterworks system was installed. He says that the people did not like to part with their water pumps, but they had to fall in line and share in the general waterworks plan. He has spoken about education and he said that when the Compulsory school education system was introduced, a number of people did not like to send their children to school but that they had to fall in line and were subject to compulsion. With those illustrations he was on perfectly sound ground, but he forgot the reason why. He himself was in those circumstances supporting compulsion. The reason was that he was making the test the good of the community, the general good. He was requiring all classes or individuals to be subject to what was conceded to be for the good of the general community. If he and I are in agreement to that extent, I think probably I can now make clear wherein I differ from him. I personally am in favour of government regulation and government control, enforced by coercion and compulsion if you wish, where it is to assert the good of the community over the good of a class, to maintain the general interest as superior to any particular interest. That is sound ground and that is the basis, where state intervention and control has been regarded as necessary, on which the Liberal party has supported compulsion and coercion in matters of government. But what is desired here in the case of this marketing legislation as proposed is the very opposite of that. What is desired here is to assert the interest of a class, and make that interest superior to the interest of the community, to make the general interest subordinate to a particular interest. May I ask the minister this question, it will illustrate
The Royal Assent

I think what we on this side who are opposing this feature of the measure have in mind. What is the basis of all representation in this parliament? It is the basis of representation by population. The representation in this House of Commons is based upon population, the entire population in given communities. It is in virtue of that fact that we are given the right to legislate for the people as a whole. But the basis of representation with regard to what is proposed by way of regulation, in other words legislation, in this bill, is not representation by population, it is representation by occupation. That fact brings out the difference. Only those who belong to a particular occupation, in one instance one class of producers, and in another instance another class of producers, are the ones who are to draw up the so-called scheme that is to govern or control. They are the ones to determine what the scheme is to be. The scheme sets forth the regulations, and these regulations, if approved, not by parliament, but by the board or minister* or governor in council, bind the whole community; also the governor in council may formulate a scheme of his own. That is where I take exception to this legislation. It does not take account of the community as a whole, nor of parliament. It takes account exclusively of the interest of one class in the community and makes that class interest superior to the interest of the community as a whole, without parliament having an opportunity either	to	approve	or	disapprove.Another doctrine that is essential if regard is to be had to our political institutions is that of ministerial responsibility. Our whole system of government	is	based upon	thedoctrine of ministerial responsibility. But here is legislation that proposes to divorce the government all but completely from responsibility. Under its provisions, the government says, we will not make the regulations, we are not the body that is going to determine what is to	be	the law	of	thiscountry, either in virtue of authority to make regulations under a general statute, or by enactment on our recommendation	by	the
House of Commons itself. We are going to leave it to different special interests to make different sets of laws to suit their own special purposes. That is a vastly different thing in the way of procedure in matters of legislation from anything we have had in the House of Commons before. Reference has been made by the government to other bills that have been introduced. For example, I think the minister himself cited the honey bill passed

at this session. It is entitled an act respecting fruit and honey. He said, this House of Commons passed that act, why should it not pass this? There is a great difference between the two measures. I have in my hand the act respecting fruit and honey, and what do I find? The regulations are all made by the minister who is a minister of the crown and whose responsibility is shared by all of his colleagues in the government, and the offences are all specifically set out in the act itself. One has only to look at the act in order to discover what the offences are. But with regard to offences to be created under this act, we do not know what they are. When this parliament prorogues we shall not know, no one will know what a week or a month hence may be an offence under the act. No one will know until one of these class groups, these occupational groups has been formed and drafted what, to serve its particular purpose, is to be in the nature of an offence. That is one great difference between any measure this parliament has previously enacted and the provisions of the measure which we are now being asked to enact.

Mr. Chairman, the minister asked me a question at the time of adjournment; I think it was as to whether I could say, with respect to the act concerning fruit and honey, what regulations would be made under the measure and what offences were created thereunder. I have a copy of the bill under my hand, and I find that under the heading "Regulations" section 3 states:
The minister may, from time to time, make regulations

Then follow paragraphs (a) (b) (c) and so on down to (1), each paragraph setting forth particular matters in connection with which the minister may make regulations, and setting them forth in a manner which makes clear to all hon. members and to the country what it is that is going to be regulated, how it is to be regulated and the extent to which it may be regulated. In some of these regulations there are specific limitations; for example in paragraph (a) I see:
-no such provision shall permit more than ten per cent of any lot of fruit to be under grade requirements;
That is informing parliament, which represents all classes in the community and the community itself as to the extent to which regulation may go, and the form and manner in which regulations are to be framed1 and carried out. But there is nothing of that kind in the proposed legislation now before us. This bill provides that some group of producers at present unknown, may prepare a scheme also of a nature at present unknown. It provides that such scheme may set forth what they propose, and wish to do or to have done, also what they propose or wish shall not be done. If that scheme is approved, then it binds the entire community and those who do not accept the regulations as set forth and which have been designated as such by the producers themselves become guilty of offences and are liable to fine and imprisonment. That is a very different thing from anything we have hitherto had.
Then I turn to the bill respecting fruit and honey in order to answer the minister's question as to whether I know what are offences under that act. I find that the bill goes farther than any other bill so far introduced in this house has gone. But on turning to the clause dealing with offences, I find its provisions in this particular are very specific. It states that no person shall do so and so and so and so, and then it sets forth in sixteen clauses the nature of offences. The offences are all specified, and this House of Commons is in a position to know, and the public is in a position to know, what is to be termed an offence. But under the legislation which we are asked to accept this house is to fix a penalty to be attached to some offence which has yet to be defined.

Or by the
minister alone, yes. It seems to me that you have two tendencies at work in this legislation, each of which is contrary to that underlying our system of government. You have, on the one hand, the tendency which is illustrated by Russia where the soviets make their laws,
not on the basis of what is in the interests of the people as a whole, but in the interests of particular occupational groups. The occupational groups determine what is to be the law with respect to matters affecting themselves, and others are made subject to the provisions of these particular laws.
The other tendency is the tendency we see in certain countries in Europe to-day, in Italy, Austria and Germany, where you have fascism; in other words, a leader taking it into his power to make whatever law he pleases and by virtue of his authority the law made binding on the rest of the community without the approval of any representative body which speaks for the community as a whole. That is the exception I take to this legislation as it has been prepared. It is not to many provisions of the bill, not to provisions that might be drafted for the purpose of regulating marketing in a way that would assist the interests of the farmers.
Hon. gentlemen say that times are changed, that the old order is yielding place to new, and that we must change conditions. That is all perfectly true, but what we have to decide is this: What is it that we want to change? Do we want to change what is basic and fundamental in our political institutions, or do we want to change economic conditions? That is the important question to ask. Do we want to change the political system of government under which British communities are accustomed to make their laws, and substitute for it something that resembles what they have in Russia, or Austria or Italy or Germany? Or do we wish to hold to British parliamentary institutions, and whatever laws we find it necessary to make, make them at least in accordance with the practice and procedure of those institutions?
Let me illustrate concretely with respect to one clause of this proposed enactment. Under British parliamentary institutions we have always held that the House of Commons had responsibility for the control of expenditures, that the House of Commons ought to control the public purse. The method of control that has been adopted has been that of obliging parliament to appropriate moneys for particular purposes. We have had that necessity discussed over and over again in this house, the necessity of parliament controlling expenditures. We on this side have taken exception to the government's course with respect to relief measures where, on the score that there was a period of distress, the government asked for a free hand. But that was claimed by the government to be in the nature of an exception required by an existing emergency.

In order to
illustrate what I have in mind, I should like to direct attention to one of the amendments being proposed by the ministry. Very strong exception was taken on this side to part II of the bill which left it to a particular group appointed not only to investigate conditions but to determine what was to be an offence.
I am glad to notice the government has taken account of the force of the exception taken to these clauses and is proposing to make a material ehange which, if I understand it aright, will meet what there was in the nature of opposition to that part of the measure. The government is proposing to do away with the word "determine" and substitute the word "report." That means that when an investigation is held a report will be made by the investigators to the minister and to the government. The report will be public, and undoubtedly will be serviceable in helping to make more effective the law with regard to preventing the undue enhancement of prices or the restraint of trade which is unreasonable and unfair. It is changes like these which help to bring this legislation more into line with what we have been contending all along should be the course to be followed. The individual is afforded knowledge of the law in advance and in the matter of prosecutions is surrounded with the protection accorded by the courts to innocent parties.
If a similar change could be made with respect to part I of this legislation, whereby these local organizations might make reports to the ministry of conditions as they exist and the ministry take the responsibility of enacting legislation or passing orders in council which would be generally known and made generally applicable from coast to coast, then so far as I am concerned I would cease to have any opposition to the measure as a measure of an experimental character. But where it is left to an unkown local board to say what is to constitute an offence, while we who are members of parliament are asked to fix in advance the penalty to be attached to unknown offences, then I say we are abandoning altogether the basis upon which all legislation should rest.
What are some of the conditions which should govern in conferring power to legislate? First of all, we have the Representation Act which provides that members to have the right to legislate shall obtain that right pro-

vided only that they represent all classes in a particular constituency. There is no such safeguard here with regard to those who are to make regulations. They may be individuals; they may be a small group in a given locality, they may be a fairly comprehensive group, but all that the Representation Act stands for, in the way of representing the community as a whole, is being swept to one side. Then we have the Elections Act which provides for a secret ballot and contains provisions which must be enforced and observed before anyone can be permitted to make the laws of the land. There is nothing here in the nature of a secret ballot. It is provided that a certain group, which may be a powerful group, shall determine what is to be done. The safeguards which the Elections Act throws around the selection of those who are to make the laws are being cast to one side. Finally we have the Franchise Act-the ministry is introducing a new one this session- which provides what individuals are entitled to have their names on the voters' lists. They are to be the ones who are to determine who shall make the laws. There is no such provision here. The laws to be enacted under this measure are to be enacted by a particular group belonging to one special occupation which comes along and draws up a scheme and asks the ministry to approve. If that scheme is approved the whole thing becomes binding, on all in a particular community, but not equally in all parts of the country. As has been said over and over again, the individuals which thus meet to frame the law are only a group representing one class in a given community. While the legislation which they pass may be for their own special interest, it is for their interest as a class, but not with regard to the interest of the community as a whole. I say that no board should be permitted to deal with matters of this kind that has not on it representation of all the classes in the community, particularly the consumers, with respect to anything in which producers are interested; because it is useless to say that you can legislate in the interests of one class without affecting those of other classes as well. We all know the interests of all classes are intertwined and interwoven in a variety of ways.
